I have been working on a game engine on and off for a while now. It has gotten to the point where you can make a simple game like pong in a matter of minutes if you know C++. It uses box2d for physics and it is an entity component based engine. I plan on adding lighting/shadows and sprite batching later on but I'm not sure what other basic things should be a part of the engine. It is a 2d engine by the way.
What basic functionality should/does every game engine offer?

Even in 2D people are going to expect to be able to make use of lighting and shaders.

Handle the mainloop for the programmer, probably have some sort of callback system for the events making use of a pervasive event queue. No having one event queue for inputs you get from the underlying library and another for collisions and other things at the game engine level; an object registers for events somehow, and they all appear the same.

You probably want a way to store previous events as well for something like a fighting game or anywhere else where the interpretation of the current event will depend on previous events. Think of a hadouken or having to press A and B at the same time.

You're going to want some sort of animation system, ideally you'll have some sort of tweening in there but I wouldn't call that essential.

Abstracted resource loading; if you let someone hard-code Windows style paths into their game, quite a few people are going to wonder why their game doesn't work when they try to port it to OSX or any other platform on the planet, which brings up...

Be portable. I understand not working with Android and iPhone, but it's really not that hard to be portable between Windows, OSX, and Linux when you start doing the work early. Just keeping both Windows and OSX will make porting to Linux much easier later, if you choose to do so or let someone else do so.

Have useful base components. Think of the sorts of games that someone is going to want to make with a 2D engine and add components for it; make sure that they're configurable enough that you can't just reskin the 1 game you made with the components. You'll want some components for shooters (8 directional or analog movement, at least 1 basic bullet), for platformers (2d movement, gravity,) puzzle games are broad enough that you can ignore them, you'll need some for UI elements (a button, a slider, a toggle...)

That's about all I can think of off the top of my head.

EDIT: The components go beyond basic functionality I guess, and you can get by without storing previous events; the objects would have to handle that themselves.
You just covered everything I love about using engines. Well done!

Well what you really want is an open event system because you don't know what sort of events your users are going to want. Someone making a platformer is probably going to want an event when the player is close enough to the edge of the screen that they need to scroll, for example.

I haven't gotten this part implemented yet in my game, but here's my idea of how it'd probably work in an ideal world; bear in mind that I've never actually worked with this system before.

What you'll probably end up doing for this is creating an Event struct or object which is stored in a hashtable or even a sparse array. You'll access the events via unique event IDs, and then something to map between friendlier strings and their current event ID. Anything can then ask to receive this type of event from whatever type of object (In component terms, any object with the FooReceiver component can register to receive Foo events from any object with a FooGenerator component.) In a FooGenerator you're just checking to see if whatever triggers a Foo event tripped then calling all of the FooReceivers that registered with you.

Good point. I think a simple way to make that is just passing a pointer to the callback function and a pointer to an event checker function. Each loop the event checker will be called for every event and it should return true or false. I can make it more robust later on so that a single event will fire multiple object's callback functions or so that you can grab an event via its id so you can have objects that monitor events and count them or something.

One thing I am trying really hard to do though is keep the required code to utilize any system in the engine down to a bare minimum without removing flexibility/control. That's one of the reasons I scrapped my old event system. Because it required you to write a function to callback AND at least 10 more lines of code. This new idea will require you to write 2 functions and at least 1 line of code to watch the event.

Maybe not a direct answer to your question, but I'm working on a game and whilst doing so I'm creating the "engine" parts as independently from my game as I can.

What I've found I've needed so far:

  1. Abstract Classes / Interface Classes for object types. These are passed to a scene manager. So you create your own classes based on a "Drawable" abstract etc; drawable objects are passed to the scene-manager.

  2. Scene Manager abstract. The one provided in the engine is derived from an Abstract class. So the user of the engine can create their own scene manager if they want.

  3. Shader Program, Texture, Mesh handling. The classes all user internal statics to keep maps of previously loaded things and use internal reference counting. This means that the user doesn't pass around pointers to things if they don't want to; which allows their game architecture to operate without the engines architecture in consideration.

  4. Very extensive UI library. It's actually bigger than the engine.

  5. Scripting for the UI and engine. This is where I'm at now.

From the top of my head? API support (for when it gets bigger and starts interacting with web services etc), logging/telemetry, custom debugging print-outs, command line support (!), general object/entity encapsulation and solid base classes from which new, custom classes can inherit from basic functionality, a robust UI system etc . . .

Also an easy to use sound engine (being able to load and play background music/sound effects). Oh and these components that are being discussed in this thread (input,sound,advanced shaders etc) should all be like plug-ins. Easy to include but also have the possibility of not using some of them if needed.
